transcript.content: Hello, welcome. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Um… I came in because I’m having a really hard time making myself go near the front windows at work, or even that part of the street outside. I work retail, so it’s not like I can just avoid the front of the store forever, but lately I keep doing exactly that. I’ll find reasons to stay in the back—like organizing stock, checking boxes, pretending something needs to be fixed—anything so I don’t have to be up by the windows or looking out onto that area.

It’s embarrassing because it’s part of my job, and I know people notice, or at least I’m worried they do. I keep telling myself I’m just being difficult or dramatic, but when I think about going over there, I just… I can’t make myself do it. That’s mostly why I’m here.
When you think about being near the front windows, do you feel a strong sense of fear or anxiety that something bad might happen?

Yeah… I mean, that’s the closest way to describe it. When I even think about standing near those front windows or being able to see that part of the street, my whole brain just kind of goes, no, don’t do that. Like it’s not just “I don’t feel like working up front today.” It feels like if I go over there, something bad could happen, or I’ll feel trapped looking out there, and I just… I can’t get myself to do it.

So I end up making all these excuses to stay in the back. I’ll suddenly decide the stockroom needs organizing, or I’ll offer to handle boxes, or I’ll make it seem like there’s something I need to check away from the front. And I know that’s not really a long-term plan, because being near the windows is part of the job, but in the moment it feels like I’m choosing between doing that or panicking. It’s hard to explain without sounding dramatic, but the fear feels really real when I’m near that area.
Can you tell me more about when this started? Have you had any experiences near the front windows or that area of the street that might explain why you feel this way now?

It started about two weeks ago. I mean, really specifically after… after a car crashed through the front window of the store during an overnight shift. That was right in that area I’m talking about, the front windows and the street outside.

Before that, I didn’t love being up front all the time or anything, but I could do my job normally. I wasn’t avoiding it like this. But since that night, it’s like that whole section of the store feels different to me. I know it’s been fixed up enough to work there, and I know it’s not happening again every time I walk over there, but my body doesn’t seem to care about that. It just connects that spot with the crash.

So yeah, it’s been about two weeks, and it’s been pretty much ever since then.

Since the car crash, have you found yourself avoiding that area of the store even when you know logically it's safe, and does thinking about the crash bring back strong memories or feelings like you're reliving it?

Yeah, I do avoid it, even when I know in my head that it’s probably safe. That’s kind of the frustrating part, because logically I can tell myself, like, the window’s been repaired, cars aren’t just going to come through every day, people are working up there and they’re fine. But when I’m actually at work, I keep steering myself away from the front without even fully deciding to at first.

Like I’ll say, “Oh, I should go check the back,” or “I’ll handle the stockroom,” or I’ll suddenly make myself busy with boxes or anything that keeps me away from the windows and that side of the street. And I know that’s part of my job, being up front, helping customers, being near the windows… but I just can’t make myself do it like I used to.

As far as the crash, thinking about it definitely brings up a strong feeling. I don’t know if I’d call it reliving it exactly, but it’s like my body remembers that spot as dangerous. Just looking toward that area or imagining standing there makes everything feel too close again, and I get this really strong urge to get away from it.

Other anxiety disorders (F40.240, F40.00, F40.10) are less likely given the clear trauma-related onset and pattern of symptoms.
